11556-facing-the-flag:
Jules Verne's Facing the Flag, in an anonymous American translation first published in 1897, opens at Healthful House, where Count d'Artigas appears and a kidnapping follows. The schooner Ebba carries the captives to sea, and Simon Hart, the engineer, keeps notes on where he is.

Back Cup, a hidden grotto, holds the secret at the heart of the tale, with Ker Karraje and Engineer Serko among its people. Verne compares the grotto with caves in Kentucky, Belgium, and elsewhere, counting domes, rivers, and cataracts. The novel is a scientific romance of invention, capture, and escape.
12449-a-reputed-changeling-or-three-seve:
Charlotte M. Yonge's tale, A Reputed Changeling, opens at Winchester. Two little girls walk home from a school kept by Frenchwomen, refugees before the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes. Talk of fairies, Gay's verses and Mother Goose tales frame a boy called ugly and ill-favoured, like Riquet with the tuft.

Is he a changeling, left by fairies in place of a stolen child, the girls ask. The novel follows three periods of seven years, testing that fancy against family life, faith and character. Yonge writes a historical tale for young readers, gentle in tone and fond of old Winchester. The changeling idea becomes a way to ask what makes a child truly one's own.
16407-under-the-dragon-flag:
James Allan, a Lancashire man who came into a large fortune young, tells what he saw and did in the war between China and Japan. He writes plainly, with no claim to fine style, and sets down scenes he took part in rather than a full history of the war. The book opens with his own back story, then moves to the fighting.

Readers get a first-hand view of a war that few English writers covered from the ground. Allan notes the odd chances that put him there, the sights of camp and battle, and the strain of life far from home. The result is a frank memoir of one man's war, told in his own unadorned voice.
19899-the-honour-of-the-flag:
W. W. Jacobs wrote The Honour of the Flag, a tale of the London river. Its man of business flourished for years in the East End. Having saved enough for his daily needs, he retired. He built a villa near the pleasant little town of Erith. The house overlooked the water. A considerable garden sloped down in front of it. Jacobs sets Thames-side comfort before his comedy starts.

Jacobs is best known for The Monkey's Paw and his night-watchman tales. His humor runs on sailors, skippers, and sly reversals. A flag's honour gives him patriotic cloth to cut comically. Erith and the river were his home waters. The tale shows his easy, exact storytelling. Few English humorists place a scene better.
23447-uncle-sam-s-boys-in-the-philippine:
H. Irving Hancock wrote this nineteen twelve boys' adventure of Uncle Sam's boys in the Philippines, following the flag against the Moros. The lads serve in the ranks, meet a Filipino dandy, gather at nipa barracks, and find plotters travelling with the flag.

Cervera's innocent shop, raids, and jungle fighting fill the chapters, with a frontispiece scene where an officer waves off a corporal's aid. Hancock writes for boys who love drill, duty, and daring, with clear talk of army life and island service. Readers should note the period view of empire and its foes, plain in the text, while enjoying the pace, the comradeship, and the young soldiers' grit under fire.
23476-churchwardens-manual-their-duties-:
George Henry, bishop of Guildford and archdeacon of Winchester, wrote this churchwardens' manual on their duties, powers, rights, and privileges, in a third edition from Simpkin and Company. A second edition had been called for within months of the first, a sign it met a want felt by clergy and wardens alike.

The manual was revised with new matter on burial laws, district churches and their mother church, and the transfer of land or buildings to trustees for mission work. Plain, orderly chapters tell wardens what they may do, must do, and must not do, from fabric and funds to burials and trusts. Church officers and historians will find a clear guide to a small but vital office in English parish life.
23485-the-old-man-s-bag:
T. W. H. Crosland and J. R. Monsell made this Dumpy Book for Children, number twenty two in the series, about an old man who lived in a wood with his wife and a quite large bag. One day he takes the bag on a walk, sees a hen in a field, and calls chuck, chuck.

The hen comes, and he pops her into the bag despite her great to do. More creatures and scrapes follow. A red policeman gives pursuit, a wife takes the bag down, and there is talk of cheap butter, apples knocked off a tree, and a suit measured for a soldier. The tale stays brisk and comic, with pictures for each turn. Small children will laugh at the bag that keeps filling and at the old man's cheerful cheek.
25188-the-flag:
Homer Greene's Flag, published in Philadelphia in 1917, is a patriotic novel that opens in a snow-covered village at a house called Bannerhall. A boy named Pen runs down the porch steps while his Aunt Millicent calls him back with news of his grandfather's train.

Family pride, a disputed tree, and a colonel's honor drive the home chapters, while later illustrations point to war service in France. Greene ties the flag to duty, sacrifice, and the older generation's example. The book speaks to American readers in the year the nation entered the First World War.
27745-the-true-story-of-the-american-fla:
John H. Fow published this 1908 study in Philadelphia with William J. Campbell, arguing that the true story of the American flag is more modest than popular legend. He opens with Rear-Admiral Preble's admission that Congress's records are silent on who designed the union of stars.

Fow traces colored stripes used for a common purpose nearly two hundred years before independence, and stars on a Massachusetts privateer's flag in November 1775. He holds that thirteen stripes were sentiment, not symbolism, and that stripe colors carry no fixed meaning beyond what imagination supplies.
2883-the-gold-bag:
Carolyn Wells wrote The Gold Bag as a detective novel narrated by a young but fairly experienced investigator. The crime at West Sedgwick opens the case, and chapters follow the Crawford house, the coroner's jury, the inquest, Florence Lloyd, and a gold bag found with yellow roses. A will, a midnight train, and the detective Fleming Stone all figure before the disclosure.

Suspicion falls on a beautiful girl whose fortune and lover seem to arrive with the crime itself, yet Philip Crawford insists she is neither principal nor accessory. A gold purse and two petals of a yellow rose mislead the jury. The novel pleases readers who enjoy a classic puzzle with romance, wills, and a careful untying of clues.
30288-sight-gag:
Larry M. Harris tells Sight Gag in Analog, May 1962, with pictures by Schoenherr. The tagline warns that brains help survival greatly, yet brains without muscle serve even worse than muscle without brains, and plain force is easily forgotten. Downstairs, the hotel register tells Fredericks that Mr. John P. Jones occupies Room 1014, but Fredericks does not believe the register and knows better.

Wherever his man is, he is not in Room 1014, and his real name is certainly not John P. Jones. Fredericks first met him under the name William K. Brady, as FBI Operative 71-054P, and wonders whether the K stands for killer. Operatives like Jones-Brady-X have as many names as jobs, and special talents, psi powers, make Fredericks mutter superman as a curse. Upstairs, in Room 1212, the superman sits and tries to relax.
30829-our-young-folks-vol-i-no-ii-februa:
Ticknor and Fields of Boston issued this February 1865 number, volume one, number two, of Our Young Folks, an illustrated magazine for boys and girls. The issue opens with David Matson, a New England tale told in prose, which its narrator links to Tennyson's Enoch Arden. In that poem a sailor returns from a desert island to find his wife wed to another man, and he keeps silent rather than cause her pain.

The magazine's own tale, the narrator says, is a similar story from his own neighborhood, about a man who left a young wife and little daughter for the sea. Young readers in 1865 would have found adventure, moral feeling, and pictures in one monthly parcel. Today the issue offers a clear view of Civil War era children's reading, in the plain, earnest style of its day.
30893-the-little-book-of-the-flag:
Eva March Tappan wrote this 1917 history of the American flag, published by Houghton Mifflin in Boston, New York, Chicago, Dallas, and San Francisco, and printed at the Riverside Press in Cambridge. Its chapters trace the flags that brought the colonists, the pine-tree flag and others, liberty and liberty poles, the land of many flags, Washington at Cambridge, and the Grand Union Flag.

Early chapters cover the English ancient flag, the meteor flag or Union Jack, Endicott cutting the cross from the flag, a flagless fort, and Dr. Cotton's decision on the cross. Later ones treat the Bedford flag, Sergeant Jasper saving the flag, the rattlesnake design, and the Philadelphia Light Horse Troop. It is a clear, patriotic history for young readers, told flag by flag.
32319-the-trail-of-the-sandhill-stag:
Ernest Thompson Seton's The Trail of the Sandhill Stag, with sixty drawings, was published in New York by Charles Scribner's Sons. Its copyright dates from 1899, with impressions running to December 1913. Seton, naturalist to the government of Manitoba and author of Wild Animals I Have Known, dedicates the book to the old-timers of Manitoba. Mrs. Grace Gallatin Thompson Seton did its designs for title-page, cover, and general make-up, and its literary revision.

To the reader, Seton writes simply: these are the best days of my life, these are my golden days. Its full-page drawings include The Track of a Mother Blacktail suddenly joined by two little ones' tracks, and The Trail in Spring. They continue with Wingless Birds, Sat Down in the Moonlit Snow, Seven Deer with their leader a wonderful buck, and The Doe Walking Slowly. Readers get a stag-tracking story from the Manitoba plain.
33154-the-telephone-an-account-of-the-ph:
Professor A. E. Dolbear of Tufts College wrote The Telephone in 1877. It is an account of electricity, magnetism, and sound as involved in the telephone's action, with directions for making a speaking telephone. Dolbear, author of The Art of Projecting, notes in his preface that popular exhibitions of the speaking telephone during the past six months, with newspaper articles, had created widespread interest. The interest was in the instrument. His book answers that interest with science a reader could test.

The volume explains the phenomena behind the telephone in plain terms, then tells how to build one. A student or amateur could hear the new wonder work in his own hands. As a record of the telephone's first year, it captures a moment when a marvel became a machine, and when readers wanted to understand it, not merely admire it.
5869-michael-s-crag:
Michael's Crag opens with a Cornish landlord and a question about a bleak place. Eustace Le Neve asks Tyrrel, musingly, whether he cares for the place himself, while gazing across a long gray moor and a wide expanse of black and stormy water. The upland plateau about the Lizard promontory seems bleak and cold, Le Neve grants, yet the question hints at attachment beneath the bleakness.

Readers enter a Cornish romance of moors, sea, and property, where landscape shapes character and choice. The novel favors atmosphere and dialogue, letting a single exchange open questions of home, duty, and love. It suits readers who enjoy regional fiction, Cornish settings, and stories where a crag and a coast become characters in their own right.
7038-personal-experiences-of-s-o-susag:
S O Susag of Minneapolis tells a few of his own experiences to show how pioneer ministers worked and how the Lord worked with them through the Holy Spirit. A photograph from about 1898 shows Susag with his wife and children. His foreword praises the burning passion for souls shown by those early workers in labors, fasting, and prayer, even when their training was limited.

The Holy Spirit gave them an unshaken faith in the Word of God, firm in the most trying and, to man, surprisingly unreasonable cases. Susag prays the book will bring faith and encouragement to souls seeking God when all other help has failed. He regrets waiting so long to write, since incidents fell out of order and many were forgotten.
9779-the-black-bag:
Louis Joseph Vance wrote The Black Bag in 1908, a romance of a ruined gentleman's adventures. Chapters follow diversions of a ruined gentleman, a mystery four-wheeler, and below bridge, with Madame L'Intrigante and desperate measures. A primer of progressive crime, stratagems and spoils, and refugees fill the middle acts. Rogues, vagabonds, and adventurers' luck close the chase.

Vance writes with brisk, picaresque verve, favoring disguise, pursuit, and wit. The black bag itself drives the plot from London streets to the Nore. A reader gets a lively Edwardian adventure, full of rogues and rescues, from a master of light suspense.
a-reputed-changeling-or-three-seventh-ye: Charlotte Mary Yonge tells a story of three periods of seven years, two centuries ago, opening with two schoolgirls at Winchester discussing an ugly, ill-favoured boy. The girls call him a changeling, quoting Gay's verse about a fairy who conveyed the true babe away and laid another in its place. Through Goody Madge, Anne Woodford, and Lucy Archfield, the novel tests fairy lore against family feeling, duty, and the slow proof of character.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferdinand-kon:
Ferdinand Konsag was a German Jesuit missionary in the missions of Lower California. Born in Croatia in 1703, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1719. He reached Mexico in 1730 and laboured chiefly in the mission of Lower California. As visitator he oversaw the whole mission with ardent zeal.

Konsag explored the coastal country as far as the Rio Colorado river. His maps, diaries, and letters shaped the later histories of California's missions. Despite delicate health, he achieved far more than seemed possible. He died in 1758, famed as a courageous explorer and cartographer.

facing-the-flag:
Verne's Facing the Flag is a novel of a stolen weapon and a pirate stronghold. Jules Verne wrote it as Face au drapeau in 1896. This text is the anonymous American translation first issued in 1897. The engineer Simon Hart narrates much of the tale in his notes.

The contents open at a place called Healthful House. Count d'Artigas arrives, and a kidnapping follows in chapter III. The schooner Ebba carries the captives to Back Cup. Ker Karraje rules that hidden base, and Engineer Serko advises him. Five weeks in Back Cup build toward a naval fight. A battle between the Sword and a tug precedes the climax. Verne mixes invention, sea power, and patriotic peril.
govdocs-archive_org-LinaJriTheFightAgain:
Juri Lina, an Estonian writer, assembled The Fight Against Usury as a history of the condemnation of lending at interest. His authorities run from Plato and Aristotle through the early Church Fathers to Goethe and Wagner. The book is a polemic built from quotations across two thousand years.

Lina marshals the long tradition that treated usury as theft and traces how the ban weakened as modern banking rose. His reading is his own, and the work is controversial, classed by critics with conspiratorial literature. It is held in the archive's collection as it stands: the usury question, polemically told, for readers studying the argument and its sources.
michael-s-crag:
Grant Allen published this novel in Chicago and New York in 1893. It carries more than three hundred and fifty silhouette illustrations by Francis and Alec Carruthers Gould. The opening chapters name a Cornish landlord and the place called Trevennack. Later chapters promise remorse, a strange delusion, and peril by land.

The chapter list shows a plot of danger and rescue on the Cornish coast. Titles like Medical Opinion and A Bold Attempt hint at injury and disputed sanity. Allen keeps the pace of a popular adventure while filling it with coastal scenery. The silhouettes give the book a striking visual character unlike ordinary illustrated novels.
nasa-tm-19660009041-electron-emission-wi:
James F Morris at Lewis Research Center wrote this journal article draft, dated December 28, 1964, on how electrons leave a hot surface. Near a surface, an electron feels a pull called the image potential. Morris studies what changes when that pull is cut off, or terminated, at some point. Transmission coefficients, which give the chance of escape, are part of the study.

Electron emission drives thermionic converters and many vacuum devices. A small change in the surface pull can change the current a great deal. Morris treats the physics in a form suited to a journal of applied physics. The work belongs to the basic research behind power devices that NASA hoped to fly.
personal-experiences-of-s-o-susag:
S. O. Susag wrote his Personal Experiences to show how the pioneer ministers worked, and how, he believed, the Lord worked with them. His foreword praises their burning passion for souls, shown in labours, fasting, and prayer. The book, first published in 1948 at Guthrie, Oklahoma, collects testimonies of outstanding answers to prayer.

A publisher's preface adds that Susag was born at Steinkjer, Norway, in 1862 and came to Minneapolis, where he kept a store before moving to Paynesville, Minnesota, in 1892. Demand kept the little book in print through a fourth edition.
podcast-joerogan-2EgPGQmhWag:
Rogan turns tour guide in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience that roams across world history. The talk moves from ancient empires and the men who conquered them to Martin Luther, the German monk whose protest split the Western church. Few podcast hours cover ground this wide.

Along the way, Rogan links the rise and fall of empires to the lives of bold, ruthless leaders. Luther's stand against Rome becomes a case study in how one person can shake a whole system. The segment works as a fast, opinionated sweep through conquest, faith, and power, told in the show's loose style.
podcast-tuckercarlson-dPEbjKiJ5ag:
Former congressman Matt Gaetz joins Tucker Carlson in Florida for a sharp political talk. They open with a clip from a Jerusalem Post event in Washington. A state official's words set off the discussion.

The title targets Senator Ted Cruz and a hoped-for 2028 run. Gaetz calls that bid delusional. They also discuss the ADL and its role in public debate. Gaetz argues identity politics now infects the right as well. The episode gives his blunt read on party fights that most officials discuss only in private. Neither man softens his words for party leaders.
the-black-bag:
Louis Joseph Vance published an adventure novel in 1908, dedicated to his mother, with illustrations by Thomas Fogarty. Chapter one is called Diversions of a Ruined Gentleman. A later heading says some people have adventures thrust upon them.

Calendar's daughter, an address at 9 Frognall Street, and the mystery of a four-wheeler follow. Chapters move below bridge, to desperate measures, and off the Nore. A primer of progressive crime, stratagems and spoils, and travels with a chaperon promise rogues and vagabonds. Illustration captions show a boy helped to his feet and a man straddling Mulready's body before two others.
the-gold-bag: Carolyn Wells wrote The Gold Bag. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list of twenty chapters. The heads open with The Crime in West Sedgwick. They open with The Crawford House. They move through an inquest. They name Florence Lloyd, yellow roses, a will, and Louis's confession. Later heads promise The Owner of the Gold Bag, a midnight train, and Fleming Stone. It is a murder mystery built around a gold bag.
under-the-dragon-flag:
James Allan's Under the Dragon Flag, published at New York in 1898, records his experiences in the Chino-Japanese War. Chapter one begins with apologies for plain writing: he claims no literary skill, only exact and unadorned remembrance of things he witnessed and took part in. A few facts about himself, he says, are necessary first.

Allan was a Lancashire gentleman's son who inherited upwards of eighty thousand pounds from the cotton trade. He ran through the fortune in under four years at Paris gaieties and Monte Carlo gaming tables. Broke and regretful, he stood at ruin's terminus when chance threw him toward China. The memoir's war reporting grows out of that spent fortune.
